extracted.intended_audience: students, philosophers of science, and scientists interested in the foundations of induction and causation
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical and methodological principles for forming, testing, and interpreting inductive generalizations and causal claims in scientific inquiry. Focuses on the nature of laws, causes, conditions, and the logical status required for inductive logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthening by inclusion in stronger laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The strong induction becomes still stronger when a weaker one has been bound up with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a previously weaker induction is shown to be a corollary of a better-established general law, the evidence for the weaker inference is not merely preserved but is increased because the independent observations that supported the weaker induction become additional evidence for the stronger law. Example: historical inductions about abuses of power gain assurance when deduced from broader facts about human character and education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of consistency with stronger inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: If an induction conflicts with stronger inductions, or with conclusions correctly deduced from them, the weaker one must give way unless the stronger inductions are unjustifiably universalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apparent empirical generalizations (e.g., beliefs in omens, oracles, astrology) are overturned when they are inconsistent with later, stronger scientific inductions about underlying causes. Conflict with well-established laws is a decisive reason to reject or revise a weaker induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual confirmation via ratiocination
rubrics_metrics.description: All inductions which can be connected by ratiocination are confirmatory of one another; the one which becomes a conclusion from ratiocination rises to at least the level of certainty of the weakest of those from which it is deduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When several inductions can be combined deductively, they mutually strengthen each other. Example: Torricelli's experiment combined three more general laws and thereby converted a doubtful generalization (the weight of the atmosphere) into a firmly established doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of certain universal, indefeasible inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: There must exist certain and universal inductions which are sufficiently certain and universal to serve as foundations for the Logic of Induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inductive logic presupposes some uniformities that are effectively exceptionless (within human purposes). Without such foundations (e.g., laws of number, space, or causation), we could not elevate other inductions to high certainty by reductive argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of laws of number and space for succession
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws of number and of space (geometry) are rigorous and universal, but they are laws of simultaneous phenomena and cannot by themselves yield laws about succession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although arithmetic and geometry provide exemplars of certainty, they do not by themselves produce truths about temporal succession (causation). To infer laws of succession we must combine spatial/numeric laws with premises that already express succession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of laws of succession for prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all truths relating to phenomena, those which relate to the order of their succession are the most valuable for anticipating future facts and for influencing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For practical prediction and control, laws describing how phenomena succeed one another (causal laws) are essential. The search for a fundamental law of succession (with indefeasibility like geometry) leads to the Law of Causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Universal Causation (foundational assumption)
rubrics_metrics.description: The law that every fact which has a beginning has a cause; the recognition that invariability of succession is found by observation to obtain between every fact in nature and some other fact which has preceded it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopting Universal Causation as co-extensive with human experience provides the basis for reducing the inductive process to rules: for any event that begins, there exists some antecedent combination invariably connected with it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical/physical definition of cause
rubrics_metrics.description: When speaking of causes the inquiry concerns physical causes—causes which are themselves phenomena and that can be gained from experience—not metaphysical efficient causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For inductive logic we only need a notion of cause expressible in empirical terms: an antecedent (or set of antecedents) that is invariably followed by the consequent, given the present constitution of things. Avoid metaphysical appeals to 'ultimate' causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause as the sum of antecedent conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The real Cause is the whole of these antecedents; we have, philosophically speaking, no right to give the name of cause to one of them exclusively of the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causal statements are incomplete unless they account for the full conjunction of positive and relevant antecedent conditions. Common practice may single out a proximate event for convenience, but accurate causal analysis should enumerate all indispensable conditions (examples: eating a dish + bodily constitution + health state).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of negative conditions (absence of counteracting causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative conditions may be summed up under one head: the absence of preventing or counteracting causes; this allows limiting the notion of cause to positive conditions with the one negative condition understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than enumerating numerous negative conditions, it is often scientifically exact to treat them collectively as 'no counteracting cause present.' This relies on the axiom that causes can be counteracted by other causes whose effects are governed by the same laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agent vs patient is a verbal distinction; treat all positive conditions as agents
rubrics_metrics.description: In most cases a distinction is drawn between something which acts (agent) and something acted upon (patient), but this distinction vanishes on examination: all positive conditions are alike agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should not privilege the 'agent' metaphysically; the so-called patient often contributes actively to the outcome and may itself be treated as an agent in causal explanations (e.g., the body's properties in response to poison).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include dispositional/preparatory states as causal effects
rubrics_metrics.description: We must include among the effects of causes the capacities given to objects of being causes of other effects (states of preparation or dispositions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causal chains often include steps that create a lasting capacity or disposition (e.g., gunpowder made explosive, paint conferring whiteness). Such predispositional states are legitimate effects of causes and must be accounted for when enumerating conditions of later phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation implies belief in invariant future connection (not mere past succession)
rubrics_metrics.description: When we define the cause to be 'the antecedent which it invariably follows,' we mean not merely the antecedent which it invariably has followed in past experience, but one we believe, as long as the present constitution of things endures, will always be so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating mere uniform past succession as causal (to prevent absurdities like night being the cause of day). Causation requires an expectation of continued invariability under current conditions, not only historical regularity.
